Q: how to fix groovy.lang.MissingMethodException: No signature of method: java.util.ArrayList.get() is applicable for argument types: () values: [] A:

If you want the list to be assigned to groupedDocs, Remove the .get() from the below line

groupedDocs = reader.selectGroupedDocs(last_update_date.toString()).get();

The get method in the list expects an argument. If you are trying to assign a particular value in the list to groupedDocs you need to pass in an index in the get method in order to retrieve it.

Eg. groupedDocs = reader.selectGroupedDocs(last_update_date.toString()).get(1);

Q: Linux shell get value of a field from a yml file A:

another awk solution, but only invoking 1 utility instead of grep + tail + awk :

development:
  adapter: mysql2
  encoding: utf8
  database: d360
  host: localhost
  username: root
  password: password

test:
  adapter: mysql2
  encoding: utf8
  database: sample
  host: localhost
  username: root
  password: password

awk '$!(NF *= $1 == "test") = $7' FS='[ \t]*:?[ \t\n]+' RS=

sample

If you're curious what that big regex in FS does, this is how it flattens each section into a single row :

awk NF=NF FS='[ \t]*:?[ \t\n]+' OFS=' | ' RS=


     1  development | adapter | mysql2 | encoding | utf8 | database | 
               d360 | host | localhost | username | root | password | password

     2  test        | adapter | mysql2 | encoding | utf8 | database | 
             sample | host | localhost | username | root | password | password

So while I've hard-coded extraction of the 7th field (i.e. column), one can technically do a linear scan of even-indexed fields/columns to locate the specific parameter they need For this to work, the biggest assumption is that there are extra blank lines between sections.

Q: How do I get Python GEKKO chemical splitter unit operation to propagate mole fractions from input to output streams? A:

The splitter propagates the inlet composition to the outlets. The issue is the direction of the outlet connect() calls, not a missing mole-fraction equation.

GEKKO documents f.connect(s1,s2) with the important rule that the first object dictates the properties of the combined object. The splitter keeps the same mole fractions while dividing the molar flow rate.

Your inlet connection is correct because the specified inlet stream should dictate the splitter inlet.

f.connect(spl_inlet, spl.inlet)

For the outlets, however, the direction should be reversed. The splitter outlet should dictate the properties of the new outlet stream:

f.connect(spl.outlet[0], spl_outlet1)
f.connect(spl.outlet[1], spl_outlet2)

instead of:

f.connect(spl_outlet1, spl.outlet[0])
f.connect(spl_outlet2, spl.outlet[1])

So the relevant part becomes:

spl_outlet1 = f.stream(fixed=False)
spl_outlet2 = f.stream(fixed=False)

# Feed -> splitter
f.connect(spl_inlet, spl.inlet)

# Splitter -> outlet streams
f.connect(spl.outlet[0], spl_outlet1)
f.connect(spl.outlet[1], spl_outlet2)

m.options.SOLVER = 1
m.solve(disp=False)

print('Outlet 1:',
      [xi.value[0] for xi in spl_outlet1.x])
print('Outlet 2:',
      [xi.value[0] for xi in spl_outlet2.x])

print('Flows:',
      spl_outlet1.ndot.value[0],
      spl_outlet2.ndot.value[0])

The expected result is approximately:

Outlet 1: [0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1]
Outlet 2: [0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1]
Flows: 2.5 7.5

With spl.split[0]=0.25, GEKKO calculates the final split as the remainder, so the second outlet receives 0.75 of the 10 kmol/s inlet. You do not need to add

m.Equation(spl_outlet1.x[i] == spl_inlet.x[i])

for each component. Those equations would reproduce the physical constraint, but the splitter object already contains that connection. It was the outlet connection order this prevents the splitter properties from being propagated.

Using each variable's .value is also the normal GEKKO way to retrieve the solved numerical value.

Q: How to remove contours with opencv? A:

Here is one way in Python OpenCV.

  • Read the input

  • Convert to grayscale

  • Threshold and invert

  • Get all contours

  • Filter contours on area

  • Sort filtered contours in increasing area

  • Remove successive contours keeping the smallest if the areas are too close in size

  • Draw contours as white on a black background

  • Get the rotated rectangles for the remaining contours

  • Draw these contours as red on copy of the input

  • Draw these contours as black on a white background

  • Save the images

Input:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input
img = cv2.imread('box_text.png')

# convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img,cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# threshold and invert
thresh = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV+cv2.THRESH_OTSU)[1]

# get all contours
contours = cv2.findContours(thresh, cv2.RETR_TREE, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]

#  filter contours to get contours larger in area than a threshold 
area_threshold = 14000
filt_contours = [cntr for cntr in contours if cv2.contourArea(cntr) > area_threshold]

# draw contours as white on a black background
cntr_img1 = np.zeros_like(thresh)
cv2.drawContours(cntr_img1, filt_contours, -1, (255), 2)

# sort contours in increasing area in order to keep the smaller of two close contours
sorted_contours = sorted(filt_contours, key=cv2.contourArea, reverse=False)

# remove successive contours that are too close in area
filt_cntrs = []
area_diff_percent = 20
for cntr in sorted_contours:
  current_area = cv2.contourArea(cntr)

  if not filt_cntrs or len(filt_cntrs) == 1:
    # keep the first two contours, since smallest two contours are too close for thresholding
    filt_cntrs.append(cntr)
  else:
    # get the previous kept contour's area
    previous_kept_area = cv2.contourArea(filt_cntrs[-1])

    # check if differences in area are greater than some threshold
    if 100 * abs(previous_kept_area - current_area) / previous_kept_area > area_diff_percent:
      filt_cntrs.append(cntr)
print(len(filt_cntrs))

# draw contours as white on a black background
cntr_img2 = np.zeros_like(thresh)
cv2.drawContours(cntr_img2, filt_cntrs, -1, (255), 2)

# get rotated rectangles and draw on copy of input and as black on white background
rotrect_img = img.copy()
rectangles_img = np.full_like(thresh, 255)
for cntr in filt_cntrs:
    # get rotated rectangle from contour
    rot_rect = cv2.minAreaRect(cntr)
    box = cv2.boxPoints(rot_rect)
    box = np.int32(box)
    # draw rotated rectangle on copy of img
    cv2.drawContours(rotrect_img,[box],0,(0,0,255),5)
    cv2.drawContours(rectangles_img,[box],0,(0),5)


# save images
cv2.imwrite('box_text_thresh.jpg', thresh)
cv2.imwrite('box_text_contours_area_filtered.jpg', cntr_img1)
cv2.imwrite('box_text_contours_successive_filtered.jpg', cntr_img2)
cv2.imwrite('box_text_rectangles_on_image.jpg', rotrect_img)
cv2.imwrite('box_text_rectangles.jpg', rectangles_img)


# show images
cv2.imshow('thresh', thresh)
cv2.imshow('contours_area_filtered', cntr_img1)
cv2.imshow('contours_successive_filtered', cntr_img2)
cv2.imshow('rectangles on image', rotrect_img)
cv2.imshow('rectangles', rectangles_img)
cv2.waitKey(0)

Q: Per-element atomicity of vector load/store and gather/scatter? A:

As of 2026, part of the answer changed after this question was asked back than in 2017.

Intel now guarantees atomic aligned 16-byte memory operations on processors which enumerate AVX, but only for legacy MOVAPD/MOVAPS/MOVDQA, their VEX.128 forms, and their EVEX.128 forms with k0 (masking disabled). The exact SDM wording is quoted in GCC's libatomic patch. AMD likewise extends atomicity a cacheable, naturally aligned single load or store from 8 to 16 bytes when AVX is reported; see section 7.3.2 of AMD APM Volume 2.

Thus those plain aligned 128-bit moves are atomic as a whole and therefore per element. No correspodning gaurantee is stated for 256- or 512-bit moves.

The answer remains no documented guarantee for masked moves. The elementwise Load_32/Load_64 pseudocode is functional notation, not a promise about memory-transaction granularity. Intel even calls the access and ordering of VMASKMOV implementation-specific for MMIO and uncached memory; VPMASKMOV omits "the access and", but in my opinion that difference is too weak and context-specific to establish per-element atomicity for cacheable memory.

The current gather documentation is clearer than it was in 2017. VPGATHERDD/QD epxlicitly warns that implementations may use loads larger than the element size or load an element more than once. Therefore FETCH_32BITS does not establish a separate 32-bit transaction. "Follows the Intel-64 memory-ordering model" orders whatever accesses the implementation pefrorms; it does not define their width or grant each pseudocode element atomicity. VPSCATTER also gives ordering and restart rules, but no per-element atomicity guarantee.

That gather warning is weaker in practice than it reads, as Peter Cordes pointed out in a comment on the current answer. Neither a wider load nor a repeated load by itself tears an element. What would tear a naturally aligned 32-bit element is assembling its value from more than one memory transaction, each narrower than the element or taken at different times. A wider load that fully contains the element delivers it untorn whenever that load is itself atomic, and loads up to a quadword that do not cross a cache line have been architecturally atomic since P6 per the "Guaranteed Atomic Operations" section (Vol. 3A, section 9.1.1, previously 8.1.1) of the Intel SDM. A containing 16-byte load is likewise atomic under the AVX guarantee above. Loading an element more than once is also harmless as long as exactly one of those loads supplies the result, and the gather pseudocode assigns each destination element from a single FETCH. The unlucky case the manual leaves open, an element stitched from sub-element pieces, does not match what measured hardware does: on Intel from Haswell on, a gather issues one load micro-op per element through the ordinary load ports, counting one element per load against the two-loads-per-cycle limit, as the uops.info port counts and Travis Downs's speed-limits analysis show, and AMD's implementations sequence gathers into ordinary element-sized loads. So for aligned elements in cacheable memory, tearing would require hardware loading bytes separately, which nothing shipped is known to do. A misaligned element that splits a cache line is where the manuals' silence carries real risk. That behavior remains a microarchitectural observation, not an architectural promise, so portable code still cannot rely on it.

So the manual-based answer is: yes for the documented aligned 128-bit plain moves; not documented for masked moves, gathers, scatters, or 256-/512-bit moves. Current hardware may be stronger: testing on Skylake and Zen 2 found aligned 128- and 256-bit VMOVDQA atomic, but that is empirical evidence rather than an architectural promise.

This conclusion addresses only hardware. In ISO C or C++, accessing atomic<int32_t> objects thruogh non-atomic SIMD operations still has language-level data-race and compiler-semantics problems.
